title: "There is no tracking information for the current branch"
summary: Set up the link between a local branch and its remote counterpart, understand what ahead/behind actually counts, and stop typing the remote and branch name every time.
mental_model: Three different things share the word 'branch': your local `main`, the server's `main`, and `origin/main` — your cached snapshot of the server's. Tracking is a config line saying which remote branch your local one is paired with.

steps.title: See who has an upstream and who does not
steps.why: main was pushed with `-u` during setup, so it has one. feature/lighting was created locally and has never met the server — it has no upstream at all.
steps.expect: main shows [origin/main]; feature/lighting shows nothing in brackets.

steps.title: Watch a bare push fail
steps.why: Git will not guess where to send a branch it has never seen. The error message is long because it is offering you the fix — but it will not act without being told.
steps.expect: fatal: The current branch feature/lighting has no upstream branch. Exit code 1.

steps.title: Push and set the upstream in one go
steps.why: `-u` (short for `--set-upstream`) pushes and records the pairing in `.git/config`. From now on, bare `git push` and `git pull` know what you mean on this branch.

verify.label: …and knows which remote branch it pairs with

steps.title: Now bare push and pull work
steps.why: The tracking config is what makes the short commands unambiguous. Nothing magical happened — two lines were written into `.git/config`.
steps.expect: ahead 1 before the push, in sync after it.

steps.title: Understand what ahead and behind count
steps.why: `ahead 1` means one commit you have that origin/main does not — as of your last fetch. It is a comparison against your cached copy, not a live query, which is why a stale clone can confidently report 'up to date' while being weeks behind.
steps.expect: 'up to date' before the fetch, 'behind 1' after it. Nothing changed on the server in between — only your knowledge of it.

steps.title: Point a branch at a differently-named remote branch
steps.why: Tracking does not require matching names. `--set-upstream-to` links any local branch to any remote one, which is how you work on `fix/thing` locally while the server calls it `renovate/thing`.
steps.expect: Fails — temp-check does not exist. Read the error, it is precise.

steps.title: Stop needing -u at all
steps.why: `push.autoSetupRemote true` makes a bare `git push` on a new branch create the remote branch and set the upstream automatically. It removes the single most common friction point in daily git.
steps.expect: A brand-new branch pushed with no flags at all.

verify.label: the new branch got an upstream without -u
feature/alerts got its upstream automatically
verify.hint: git config --global push.autoSetupRemote true, then git push

verify.label: the config that makes -u unnecessary is set
both branches exist on the server

pitfalls: `git status` reporting 'up to date' only means 'up to date with what I last fetched'. Fetch first, then believe it.
Deleting a local branch does not delete the remote one, and vice versa. They are separate objects joined only by a config line.
`git branch -vv` showing `[origin/x: gone]` means the remote branch was deleted — run `git fetch --prune` and clean up the local one.
`push.default simple` refuses to push a branch to a differently-named remote branch by accident. Keep it on.
cheatsheet: one-line ahead/behind for the current branch
refresh what ahead/behind is measured against
